newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi floodwaters surge toward Baton Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi floodwaters surge toward Baton Rouge.

text.p: Floodwaters continued to surge down the Mississippi River Thursday, forcing evacuations in low-lying areas as the river's crest approached Baton Rouge, officials said.

The river crested at Natchez, Miss., today and was expected to crest Friday in Baton Rouge, where floodwaters were lapping at the top of a sand-bag reinforced levee protecting the city's historic downtown.

Backwater flooding along tributaries feeding into the great river closed roads and forced hundreds of families to move to emergency shelters on higher ground in central and southern Louisiana, the officials said.

"This is by far the highest flow since 1930 during March," U.S. Army Corps of Engineers spokesman Rob Brown said. The river was flowing at 2.1 million cubic feet a second past Baton Rouge, two months ahead of the normal spring crest.

In Catahoula Parish northeast of Alexandria, La., three Red Cross shelters were opened and more than 75 families were evacuated as tributaries spilled over their banks. Backwater flooding also forced about 100 families to flee low-lying areas in Concordia Parish outside the Mississippi levee system, officials said.
Further downriver, Army engineers have opened 298 of the 350 flood bays on the Bonnet Carre Spillway above New Orleans to alleviate flooding in the Crescent City.
"This is a very full, dynamic river passing by here," Brown said from his New Orleans office overlooking the river.
Emergency plans were being reviewed in parishes along the length of the river, which was expected to crest at 44 feet at Baton Rouge, where a three-foot sandbag wall was added to protect downtown.

"Everything is holding up real fine," said Mike Logue, Army Corps of Engineers spokesman in Vicksburg. "At this point, the flood control system is working as it's supposed to ... we'll just have to wait and see what the weather does."
After cresting earlier this week at Vicksburg at 49.1 feet -- about six feet below the top of the downtown levee -- the river today began falling there for the first time in months, he said.

At Baton Rouge, crews worked to attach rigging to move a capsized barge that has spewed noxious fumes and delayed shipping since Monday. It was part of a tow of 25 barges that hit a bridge in the fast-moving, flood-swollen river currents.
